<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-framed cases: B on physics/prevention ("punishment requires a prior catch; geometry requires nothing of the driver") and A on coverage and incapacitation ("a consequence attaches to the person; concrete waits at one intersection"). A won the more decisive exchanges. First, A's opening reframe of penalties as incapacitation (interlock, revocation, impoundment) rather than a gamble pre-empted B's certainty/severity attack and forced B into the weaker claim that interlocks are "reactive" — which A neutralized by noting redesign is also triggered by prior deaths and covers only forty feet of asphalt. Second, A converted B's own rebuttal material into a concession twice: B admitted the lower-limit half of the motion only bites when it triggers engineering changes, and B's answer for "what protects the unrebuilt street tonight" included automated speed cameras — a certainty-of-consequence tool. B's closing distinction (low-severity automatic consequence vs courtroom post-crash sanction) was a fair and necessary repair, but it arrived late and left A's "prevention has to borrow consequences" frame partially standing. On pressure, A answered both of B's questions directly and crisply (existing courts/DMV as sunk assets versus pouring concrete block by block was the cleanest single answer in the debate), while B's response to A's arterial-mileage question was semi-evasive — "whatever fraction... the same layer" — never confronting A's repeated point that cheap humps and paint do not fix arterials, where the deaths concentrate. B left its best epistemic weapon underused: that the motion concerns *harsher* penalties, so A's reliance on ordinary general deterrence in A4.1 is off-target and mildly inconsistent with A's own dismissal of the deterrence-calculation model. That unexploited gap keeps the margin competitive rather than solid.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's handling of B's speed-camera concession: by pointing out that PRO's fastest, most scalable citywide tool is a fine-and-points machine, A forced B either to abandon it (leaving "paint and a lower number") or to concede that credible consequences do the work. B's closing distinction between automatic low-severity enforcement and post-crash punishment was the best available answer but only partly defused the hit.</best_rebuttal>
